data.title: Vitiligo — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 16 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Vitiligo** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. Define vitiligo.**
- Acquired, chronic depigmenting disorder characterised by well-defined milky-white (amelanotic) macules and patches due to selective loss of functional melanocytes from the epidermis and/or hair follicles
- Prevalence ~0.5–2% worldwide; India 0.5–2.5% (higher in Gujarat, Rajasthan); no sex predilection; ~50% begin before 20 years

**Q2. Describe melanogenesis briefly and the role of melanocytes in depigmentary disorders (PYQ).**
- Melanocytes (neural crest origin) in basal layer, ratio ~1:36 keratinocytes (epidermal melanin unit); tyrosine → DOPA → dopaquinone (tyrosinase) → eumelanin (brown-black, via TRP-1, TRP-2/DCT) or pheomelanin (red-yellow, with cysteine); melanosomes (stages I–IV) transferred to keratinocytes via dendrites
- Regulation: MC1R (α-MSH), SCF/c-KIT, endothelin-1, HGF, bFGF, UV via p53-POMC; Wnt/β-catenin, MITF master regulator
- Depigmentary disorders: absent melanocytes (vitiligo, piebaldism, Waardenburg), normal melanocytes with reduced melanin (albinism — tyrosinase defect, nevus depigmentosus — transfer defect, pityriasis alba, PIH), destroyed melanocytes (chemical leucoderma, leprosy, scars)

**Q3. Discuss current concepts in aetiopathogenesis (PYQ).**
- Convergence theory — combination of: (1) genetic susceptibility (polygenic — NLRP1, PTPN22, TYR, HLA-A*02, FOXP3; ~20% family history); (2) melanocyte intrinsic defects — oxidative stress (H2O2 accumulation, low catalase), unfolded protein response, impaired adhesion (melanocytorrhagy — reduced E-cadherin, DDR1); (3) autoimmunity — innate (HSP70i, NK cells, IL-1β, NLRP inflammasome) and adaptive — melanocyte-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells producing IFN-γ → keratinocyte CXCL9/10 → CXCR3 recruitment (JAK–STAT pathway — basis of JAK inhibitors); resident memory T cells explain relapse at same sites; reduced Tregs
- Other theories: neural (segmental — neurochemical mediators), biochemical (tetrahydrobiopterin, catecholamines), viral, intrinsic adhesion defect

**Q4. Classify vitiligo (VGICC 2012).**
- Non-segmental vitiligo (NSV — 'vitiligo'): acrofacial, mucosal (≥2 sites), generalised (vulgaris), universal (>80% BSA), mixed (NSV + SV), rare variants (punctata, minor/hypochromic, follicular)
- Segmental vitiligo (SV): uni-, bi- or plurisegmental — early onset, rapid spread then stable, leukotrichia common, poor response to medical therapy but excellent to grafting
- Unclassified/undetermined: focal (isolated macule not segmental, <2 years), mucosal (single site)

**Q5. How do you assess activity and stability?**
- Signs of activity: Koebner phenomenon (type IIb — experimentally induced; VIDA), confetti-like depigmentation, trichrome/quadrichrome/pentachrome patches, inflammatory vitiligo (raised red border), ill-defined borders, new lesions/enlargement in last 3–12 months
- VIDA (Vitiligo Disease Activity score): +4 active in ≤6 weeks, +3 in 6 weeks–3 months, +2 in 3–6 months, +1 in 6–12 months, 0 stable ≥1 year, −1 stable with spontaneous repigmentation ≥1 year
- Extent: VASI (Vitiligo Area Scoring Index — hand units × % depigmentation), VETF, F-VASI/T-VASI; VitiQoL for quality of life
- Dermoscopy: active — trichrome, starburst/comet-tail, micro-Koebner; stable — sharp border, perifollicular pigmentation (repigmenting), reversed pigment network

**Q6. What is the Wood's lamp finding and its use?**
- 365 nm UVA: bright chalk-white (blue-white) fluorescence of depigmented skin with sharp border — accentuates lesions in fair skin, distinguishes depigmentation (vitiligo) from hypopigmentation (dull off-white), helps monitor activity and repigmentation

**Q7. Associated diseases.**
- Autoimmune thyroid disease (commonest — Hashimoto's, Graves'), alopecia areata, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Addison's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, psoriasis, myasthenia gravis, inflammatory bowel disease, APS (autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes)
- Eye: uveitis, retinal pigment changes; ear: sensorineural hearing loss (rare)
- Syndromes: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (uveitis, meningism, dysacusis, vitiligo, poliosis), Alezzandrini (unilateral facial vitiligo, poliosis, retinitis, deafness)

**Q8. Differential diagnosis.**
- Congenital: piebaldism (white forelock, stable from birth), nevus depigmentosus (off-white, stable), Waardenburg, tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf), hypomelanosis of Ito
- Acquired hypopigmentation: pityriasis alba, pityriasis versicolor, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, indeterminate/ tuberculoid leprosy (sensory loss), idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis, progressive macular hypomelanosis, hypopigmented MF
- Depigmentation: chemical leucoderma (para-tertiary butyl phenol, monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone, bindi/footwear adhesives — confetti macules at contact site), DLE, lichen sclerosus, morphoea, scars, halo naevus, leucoderma in melanoma (immunotherapy-related)

**Q9. Histopathology.**
- Absence of melanocytes and melanin in lesional epidermis (confirmed with Fontana–Masson, MART-1/Melan-A, HMB-45 immunostaining); active border — superficial perivascular and lichenoid lymphocytes (CD8)

**Q10. Investigations.**
- Clinical diagnosis with Wood's lamp; thyroid function and anti-TPO antibodies (annually if positive), CBC, fasting glucose, vitamin B12 if indicated; biopsy only if doubtful

**Q11. Discuss therapeutic options in vitiligo (PYQ).**
- Halting activity: oral mini-pulse (OMP) — betamethasone/dexamethasone 5 mg on 2 consecutive days per week for 3–6 months (Pasricha), short oral steroids; methotrexate, minocycline, azathioprine, cyclosporine for rapidly progressive disease
- Topical: potent/mid-potency corticosteroids (limited/extra-facial), calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.1% — face, neck, genitals), ruxolitinib 1.5% cream (topical JAK — FDA 2022 for NSV ≥12 y), calcipotriol (with steroid), topical PUVA/psoralen + sunlight (PUVAsol)
- Phototherapy: NB-UVB (311 nm, 2–3 times/week — first line for generalised; ≥6–12 months; best on face, neck, trunk; poor on acral and lips), excimer laser/light 308 nm (targeted, localised), PUVA (older)
- Systemic JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib, ritlecitinib, upadacitinib) with phototherapy — emerging
- Antioxidants (Polypodium leucotomos, vitamin E, ginkgo biloba, α-lipoic acid), afamelanotide (with NB-UVB) — adjuncts
- Depigmentation for extensive (>50–80%) recalcitrant disease: monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone 20%, 4-methoxyphenol, Q-switched ruby/alexandrite laser, cryotherapy
- Camouflage (cosmetic cover, dihydroxyacetone, micropigmentation/tattooing for lips), counselling, support groups

**Q12. Discuss surgical management of vitiligo (PYQ).**
- Indications: stable vitiligo (no new lesion/extension for ≥1 year; positive minigraft test — repigmentation spread from a test graft after 3 months), segmental and focal vitiligo, resistant areas after medical therapy; avoid in keloid tendency and active disease
- Tissue grafts: punch/mini-punch grafting (1–1.5 mm; cobblestoning side effect), split-thickness skin grafting (thin STSG — good for large areas), suction blister epidermal grafting (best cosmetic match, no scarring at recipient), hair follicle grafts (leucotrichia)
- Cellular grafts: non-cultured epidermal cell suspension (melanocyte–keratinocyte transplantation, MKTP/ReCell), non-cultured extracted hair follicle outer root sheath cell suspension, cultured melanocytes
- Post-operative NB-UVB/PUVAsol improves results; complications — infection, cobblestoning, colour mismatch, Koebner at donor site, graft rejection; lips and acral areas respond less

**Q13. What is leucotrichia's significance?**
- White hairs in vitiligo patches indicate loss of the follicular melanocyte reservoir — poor prognosis for medical repigmentation (repigmentation normally starts perifollicularly); surgical approaches preferred

**Q14. Prognostic factors.**
- Good: recent onset, younger age, face/neck/trunk lesions, perifollicular repigmentation, dark hair in patches, NSV of short duration
- Poor: acral and lip (lip-tip) vitiligo, mucosal, leucotrichia, long duration, segmental (medically), Koebner positivity, family history, associated autoimmunity, universal type

**Q15. Genetic causes of hypomelanosis (PYQ).**
- Absent melanocytes: piebaldism (KIT), Waardenburg (PAX3, MITF, SOX10, EDNRB/EDN3), Tietz syndrome
- Abnormal melanin synthesis: oculocutaneous albinism (OCA1 TYR, OCA2 OCA2/P gene, OCA3 TYRP1, OCA4 SLC45A2), phenylketonuria
- Melanosome biogenesis/transfer: Hermansky–Pudlak (bleeding, pulmonary fibrosis), Chédiak–Higashi (giant granules, infections), Griscelli (silvery hair)
- Mosaic: hypomelanosis of Ito, nevus depigmentosus; tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules), incontinentia pigmenti (stage 4)

**Q16. Discuss Waardenburg syndrome (PYQ).**
- Autosomal dominant neural-crest disorder: white forelock, congenital sensorineural deafness, heterochromia iridis/ brilliant blue eyes, depigmented patches (piebald-like)
- Types: WS1 (PAX3, dystopia canthorum — lateral displacement of inner canthi), WS2 (MITF/SOX10, no dystopia — deafness commoner), WS3/Klein–Waardenburg (PAX3, limb anomalies), WS4/Shah–Waardenburg (EDNRB/EDN3/SOX10 — with Hirschsprung disease)

## Quick spotter facts
- Chalk-white sharply defined patch with Wood's lamp accentuation — vitiligo
- Trichrome, confetti and Koebner — active disease
- Stability ≥1 year before grafting

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Vitiligo); Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference (VGICC) 2012 classification. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
